theme: Hide me from the wicked; make haste, O God, to deliver me
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 64 and Psalm 70. One is a prayer against slander and secret plots, and the other is a short cry for speedy help. Notice how each ends with confidence.
settingTheScene: These two psalms are attributed to David and belong to the years of his persecution. Psalm 64 speaks of hidden enemies who sharpen their tongues like swords, and Psalm 70 is a five-verse petition, repeated almost word for word in Psalm 40:13-17. Both are brief, urgent, and honest.
observation: “Hear my voice, O God, in my complaint; preserve my life from dread of the enemy” (64:1).
“Who whet their tongues like swords, who aim bitter words like arrows” (64:3).
“They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, Who can see them?” (64:5).
“But God shoots his arrow at them; they are wounded suddenly” (64:7).
“Then all mankind fears; they tell what God has brought about and ponder what he has done” (64:9).
“Let the righteous one rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in him!” (64:10).
“Make haste, O God, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me!” (70:1).
“But I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God! You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay!” (70:5).
interpretation:
Psalm 64 is about the weapon of the tongue. David’s enemies do not use swords. They use words, and they use them in secret. “They talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, Who can see them?” It is the voice of a conspiracy, of whispering and plotting. Slander is among the oldest weapons, and it is hard to defend against because it works in the dark.

David’s answer is to bring the matter to God, who sees what is hidden. The whole psalm turns on the reversal of verse 7. The enemies shoot arrows from ambush, but God shoots an arrow at them. The ones who thought no one could see them are seen. “They are wounded suddenly.” The tongues they used against others are turned back on themselves.

The result is awe. All mankind fears, and tells what God has done. The justice of God, when it falls, is a lesson to the world. And the righteous rejoice and take refuge. The psalm ends not with revenge, but with refuge.

Psalm 70 is shorter and more urgent. “Make haste” appears twice. David is in an emergency, and he does not pretend otherwise. His request is simple: help me, now. He describes himself as “poor and needy.” It is the best position from which to pray. The person who knows they have nothing to offer can only receive.

Even in this hurried prayer, there is room for the praise of others: “May all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you! May those who love your salvation say evermore, God is great!” David cannot help thinking of others.

Together these prayers teach us two things. First, God sees what is done in secret. Second, we may pray urgently and simply, and we do not need elaborate words.
connection: James 3:5-8 calls the tongue a fire and a restless evil, and Jesus warned that we will give an account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36). He was himself the target of plots made in secret (Mark 14:1). Psalm 64:3 is echoed in Revelation, and the “arrow” language has a New Testament counterpart in Romans 12:19. The poor and needy have a special place with Christ (Matthew 5:3; 2 Corinthians 8:9).
application:
If you have been the target of gossip, bring it to God. He sees what is hidden.

Examine your own tongue. Is there a whisper you should stop?

When you need help urgently, pray Psalm 70:5 as a short prayer.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to protect you from slander and to keep your tongue from harming others.
Tell him you are poor and needy.
Ask him to hasten to help you.
